title: Dispensable Effort
text:
Social loafing research showed that people work less hard in groups. Norbert Kerr and Steven Bruun wanted to understand one reason why: people may hold back when they believe their effort will not change the group's result.

In their experiments, people worked in pairs or small groups on physically tiring tasks. The researchers varied the rule for how the group's score was calculated. Under one rule, the group's score was that of its best member, so only the strongest person really counted. Under another, the group's score was that of its weakest member, so the result depended on whoever did least well. Participants also learned how their ability compared with that of their partners.

Effort followed the rule closely. When the best member's score counted, the less able members, knowing their effort was unlikely to matter, reduced their effort. When the weakest member's score counted, it was the more able members who eased off, since the group's result would be limited by the weakest anyway. In each case, people slacked when they saw their own contribution as dispensable to the group's success.

Kerr and Bruun called these free-rider effects: people were not simply lazy but responding to whether their effort could actually make a difference.
lesson: People ease off when they think the result does not depend on them. Show each team member how their specific effort shapes the outcome.
source: Kerr, N. L., and Bruun, S. E. (1983). Dispensability of member effort and group motivation losses: Free-rider effects. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 44(1), 78-94.
